nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Mutton Snapper
Scientific Name:  Lutjanus analis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Lutjanidae

Other Common Names:  Pargo Cebadai, Pargo Criollo

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Cuvier 1828).
	Reference for Classification (1914)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Food fish throughout its range (2523), sold in commercial fisheries, of east and southeast Florida and the Caribbean (2414)
Recreational:  Excellent recreational food fish (2523).
Ecological:  Juvenile mutton snapper are seasonally abundant, though present throughout the year within ocean inlet seagrass meadows of the Indian River Lagoon.  Adults are commonly encountered on reefs of adjacent waters (848, 993).  High local abundance and year round presence within the Indian River Lagoon allows this top predator to influence mortality rates in certain crustacean and fish populations and therefore act as a keystone species in structuring aquatic communities, particularly near ocean inlets (2414; 2361; 2513; 2522; 993; Gilmore unpub. data).
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Adults commonly encountered on reef formations and adjacent sand bottom in neritic waters from east-central Florida, Bahama Islands and Antilles, southern Gulf of Mexico (Laguna de Terminos) to northern South American and to Cabo Branco, San Sebastian Brazil (2414; 2523; 2531; 2504; 848, 993).  No significant occurrence north of east Florida, nor in the eastern and northern Gulf of Mexico (312; 2323; 327; 2410, 2536; 664; 2146).

nodes.body:
Egg: Eggs and larvae are planktonic over the continental shelf dispersing from specific spawning sites and make diel migrations into the neuston at night from diurnal positions closer to the bottom (2514; 2517).

Salinity: recorded salinities of 4.5-37.3 ppt (887).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Most likely gonochoristic as are most other Lutjanus spp., oviparous polygamous serial iteroparous broadcast spawner (2514).
Mating/Spawning: Although there are no studies of spawning time, location, frequency or seasonality in L. analis specifically, congeners, (including L. synagris and L. griseus) have been observed spawning on new and/or full moons in early or late evening at specific sites on the continental shelf or near reef formations (2532; 672; 2507; 2524; 2511; 2412; 2514). nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  No information specifically on L. analis but  snappers of the genus Lutjanus produce 0.65-1.02 mm diameter pelagic eggs (most <0.85 mm) with a smooth chorion and unsegmented yolk and single 0.12-0.20 mm colorless oil droplet, which is located on the anterior end of the yolksac in larva (2517). nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: There is no information on the feeding habits of larval mutton snapper.  Larvae are presumed to be planktivorous. Crustaceans were predominately portunid, xanthid, calapid, and majid crabs, although penaeid/stomatopod shrimp, lobsters and anuran crabs are also comumed (2361; 2522).  Fishes consumed consisted principally of reef associates including cornetfish (Fistularia), scorpionfish (Scorpeana) squirrelfish (Holocentrus), grunts (Haemulon), wrasses (Halichoeres), parrotfish (Scaridae), surgeonfish (Acanthurus), gobies (Gobiidae), and a variety of plectognaths (Monacanthus, Sphoeroides, Diodon)(2361; 2522). nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its size the mutton snapper may influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range.  However, the foraging range is not known.  If snapper populations are reduced by anthropogenic factors it is possible that prey and competitor abundance will be influenced as has been demonstrated in certain fisheries (2513).  This community instability is inherent with the absence of "keystone" species which influence a wide variety of lower trophic levels.
Factors Influencing Populations:  Recent studies of mutton snapper fisheries off the east coast of Florida have indicated that mutton snapper did not recruit to the headboat fishery until after age 3 and as of 1985 75% of the maximum yield-per-recruit was being harvested (2521).  Mutton snapper from Cuban commercial fishermen were younger than Florida fishes landed with 85% at ages 1-4 (2534).  As with other slow growing, long lived  species, mutton snapper are particularly vulnerable to overfishing, particularly large, intensive fisheries (2521).

Predation:  Due to its size the mutton snapper may influence a variety of prey species within its foraging range.  However, the foraging range is not known.  If snapper populations are reduced by anthropogenic factors it is possible that prey and competitor abundance will be influenced as has been demonstrated in certain fisheries (2513).  This community instability is inherent with the absence of "keystone" species which influence a wide variety of lower trophic levels.
Factors Influencing Populations:  Recent studies of mutton snapper fisheries off the east coast of Florida have indicated that mutton snapper did not recruit to the headboat fishery until after age 3 and as of 1985 75% of the maximum yield-per-recruit was being harvested (2521).  Mutton snapper from Cuban commercial fishermen were younger than Florida fishes landed with 85% at ages 1-4 (2534).  As with other slow growing, long lived  species, mutton snapper are particularly vulnerable to overfishing, particularly large, intensive fisheries (2521).
